blocks.text: 大多数软件都充斥着漏洞，而 AI 现在可以轻松地发现并利用它们。针对网络攻击的标准防御手段已不再足够：我们需要能够证明代码没有漏洞的方法。形式化软件验证可以提供这种保证，但它在历史上需要专家投入数年努力，对大多数现实项目而言并不实用。然而，在与 Theorem 的合作中，我们表明情况已不再如此：LLM 现在可以大规模生成形式化证明，从而支持包含可证明安全保证的新软件开发工作流。借助 Claude，我们在 100 多个真实世界开源软件库中，于汇编代码层面（RISC-V）证明了安全属性。据我们所知，这是首次大规模尝试使用 AI 将形式化验证应用于汇编代码层面的生产软件。在编写证明的过程中，Claude 还发现了多年来一直未被检测到的漏洞，尽管已经进行了数万亿次测试运行。随着模型能力持续提升，我们预计形式化验证将成为安全软件开发中不可或缺的一部分。

blocks.text: 即使是成熟且经过大量测试的软件也包含漏洞，而 LLM 越来越擅长发现它们。Linux 内核——当今测试最充分的软件之一，部署在全球数十亿台设备上——最近披露了超过 1,000 个漏洞。随着前沿模型越来越有能力将看似无害的漏洞串联成严重漏洞利用，我们需要能够在这些漏洞于现实世界中被利用之前检测并修复它们的技术。

blocks.text: 理想情况下，这类技术能够发现并修补所有漏洞，然后提供某种证明，表明再也找不到更多漏洞了。形式化验证是实现这一点的一种方法。在形式化验证中，开发者将代码转换为数学模型，然后尝试证明它始终遵循某组已定义的安全规则。如果无法证明这一点，就意味着代码中可能存在违反规则的漏洞，而失败的性质暗示了漏洞可能是什么。重复这一过程（每次消除失败原因之后），最终将产生证明，表明代码中不存在任何会违反这些规则的漏洞。

blocks.text: 然而，形式化验证并不容易。证明可能比原始代码大许多倍，编写证明需要大量努力以及小众且高度专业化的技能组合。例如，实现 seL4 操作系统内核花费了两人年，但对其进行形式化验证花费了20人年。因此，形式化验证仅在真正关键任务的应用中才具有实用性，例如空客的航空电子代码。

blocks.text: 但 LLM 让这件事变得容易得多。前沿模型现在能够完全自主地为真实世界的软件生成正确性证明。为了演示这一点，我们让 Claude 为 123 个开源库证明有用的安全属性，包括证明它们的某些可执行产物在某些条件下绝不会崩溃。具体而言，Claude 证明了：在特定假设下（即程序以单线程静态二进制形式运行、内存预算固定、运行在采用 Linux 操作系统的 RISC-V1 CPU 上），对于所有小于 64 MB 的输入以及所有建模的 Linux 操作系统（OS）响应和内存布局，这些程序将始终正常退出，不会触发内存安全错误或断言失败。这距离修复所有可能的 bug 仍很遥远，但确实让我们比以往更接近目标，并提供了通往该目标的路线图。

blocks.text: 要证明一段软件是正确的，我们首先必须说明“正确”究竟意味着什么。正确性由规约（spec）定义。在某些程序中，有一种清晰的方式来形式化地规定程序的预期行为。例如，PNG 解码器接收一串字节，并（遵循 RFC 2083）将这些字节解码为对应的图像。但对于大多数程序来说，事情并没有这么简单。文本编辑器或网页浏览器“正确”意味着什么？获得全面且无歧义的规约的难度，是在更大规模上验证软件的一大障碍。

blocks.text: 为了针对我们试图证明的开源库代码解决这一问题，我们采取的方法是：自动将其已有的可编译测试套件转换为一份规范，具体做法是把“该测试套件始终通过”这一规则编码进去，并采用一个通用模型来刻画在 Linux 上执行任何 RISC-V 编译二进制文件的含义。从历史上看，证明这类规范一直是难以处理的，原因在于编写一个能够涵盖并论证数万条汇编指令在任意输入下的所有可能行为和交互的证明本身具有内在复杂性（以及由此导致证明往往极其庞大）。这正是当今 LLM 的用武之地：为达成一个定义明确的目标而处理数百万行代码，正是 LLM 极其擅长的事情。

blocks.text: 在几周的时间里，Claude 成功修补了它发现的漏洞，随后证明：对于 123 个不同 OSS-Fuzz 库中的 239 个入口点，在任何输入（最大 64 MB）下都不会发生崩溃。这些证明作用于编译后的 RISC-V 指令（即可执行二进制文件），总计约 1.8 亿行 Rocq 代码，典型证明约 60 万行，为二进制文件提供安全保障，而这些二进制文件的中位长度为 18,000 条 RISC-V 指令。这些证明是通过使用 Theorem 的 RISC-V 指令和 Linux 进程语义，将 RISC-V 汇编代码转换为数学模型而构建的。这意味着这些证明目前假设程序在运行 Linux 操作系统的 RISC-V CPU 上，以单线程静态二进制形式运行，并具有固定的内存预算。扩大这些证明的范围完全触手可及，因为这将涉及为更多汇编架构和其他操作系统进程标准化语义。请参阅专家对 Claude 所写证明的评论。

blocks.text: 证明超越内存安全

inlines.text: 证明超越内存安全

blocks.text: 证明一个模糊测试不再有崩溃可被发现，其意义比听起来更大。在现实世界的代码中，模糊测试常常用于检验有意义的高层属性是否被违反，例如编码-解码往返、幂等性、代数定律、差分测试、自洽性或与参考实现的等价性。例如，针对 LZO 压缩算法的模糊测试断言：如果你压缩一个输入，然后解压它，结果与原始输入相同。如果该属性不成立，程序就会崩溃——因此证明测试永不崩溃，就等同于证明该属性本身。

blocks.text: Most software is riddled with bugs, which AI can now easily find and exploit. The standard defenses against cyberattacks are no longer sufficient: we need ways to prove that code is free of bugs. Formal software verification could provide this guarantee, but it has historically required years of expert effort, making it impractical for most real-world projects. In a collaboration with Theorem, however, we show this is no longer the case: LLMs can now produce formal proofs at large scale, enabling new software development workflows that include proven security guarantees. Using Claude, we proved security properties at the assembly code level (RISC-V) in over 100 real-world open-source software libraries. To our knowledge, this represents the first large-scale effort to use AI to apply formal verification to production software at the assembly code level. While writing the proofs, Claude also discovered bugs that had eluded detection for years, despite trillions of test runs. As model capabilities continue to improve, we expect formal verification to become an essential part of secure software development.

blocks.text: Introduction

inlines.text: Introduction

blocks.text: Even mature, heavily tested software contains bugs, and LLMs are increasingly adept at finding them. The Linux kernel—one of the most well-tested pieces of software today, deployed on billions of devices worldwide—recently had over 1,000 vulnerabilities disclosed. With frontier models becoming more capable of chaining seemingly benign bugs into critical exploits, we need techniques that can detect and fix these bugs before they can be exploited in the wild.

blocks.text: Ideally, such techniques could find and patch all bugs, and then provide some proof that there are no more to be found. Formal verification is one way to do this. In formal verification, developers translate their code into a mathematical model, then try to prove that it always follows some defined set of security rules. If they fail to prove this, that means there could be a bug in the code that would violate a rule, and the nature of the failure implies what the bug might be. Repeating this process (after eliminating the cause of failure each time) will ultimately yield proof that the code is devoid of any bug that would violate those rules.

For instance, it took two person-years to implement the seL4 operating system kernel, but 20 person-years to formally verify it. Accordingly, formal verification has been practical only in truly mission-critical applications, such as Airbus’s avionics code.

blocks.text: Turning tests into proofs

inlines.text: Turning tests into proofs

blocks.text: To prove that a piece of software is correct, we must first state what “correct” even means. Correctness is defined by the specification (spec). In some programs, there is a clear way to formally specify the program’s intended behavior. For example, a PNG decoder takes a sequence of bytes and (following RFC 2083) decodes these bytes into the corresponding image. But for most programs, things aren’t so straightforward. What would it mean for a text editor or a web browser to be “correct”? The difficulty of obtaining a comprehensive and unambiguous spec is a significant obstacle to verifying software at a larger scale.

blocks.text: To address this for the code in the open-source libraries that we sought to prove, we take the approach of automatically converting their preexisting compilable test suites into a spec by encoding the rule “this test suite always passes,” using a general model of what it means to execute any RISC-V-compiled binary on Linux. Historically, proving such specs was intractable, given the inherent complexity of writing a proof that can encompass and make an argument over all possible behaviors and interactions of tens of thousands of assembly instructions over any input (and the fact that proofs tend to be extremely large as a result). This is where today’s LLMs come in: churning through millions of lines of code in pursuit of a well-defined goal is a task that LLMs are extremely well suited for.

blocks.text: For this project, we started with fuzz tests. In these tests, developers write an entry point2 into their code that takes inputs, such that any input that causes a crash is a bug the authors care about. Then the fuzzer, a testing engine, generates enormous numbers of semirandom and mutated inputs at the entry point to try to find a bug (visualized in Figure 1). The longer a fuzzer runs, the more bugs it can find. But this is inherently a brute-force process, with no guarantee of exercising every possible code path, regardless of how many inputs you try.

blocks.text: We did this for hundreds of projects in Google’s OSS-Fuzz initiative, which provides continuous fuzz testing for qualifying open-source projects. OSS-Fuzz contains thousands of developer-authored entry points that look for broken code properties by crashing (for example, on a failed assertion). OSS-Fuzz automatically instruments C and C++ programs with AddressSanitizer4 (ASan), causing them to crash whenever memory is accessed improperly (which is a leading cause of software vulnerabilities). Broad-spectrum specifications like memory safety apply to almost all software.

blocks.text: Over the span of a few weeks, Claude successfully patched the bugs it found and then proved that there are no crashes on any input (up to 64 MB) for 239 entry points across 123 different OSS-Fuzz libraries. These proofs operate on the compiled RISC-V instructions (i.e., executable binaries), and they comprise about 180 million lines of Rocq, with a typical proof running to about 600,000 lines to provide security guarantees on binaries with a median length of 18,000 RISC-V instructions. These proofs are built by translating the RISC-V assembly code to a mathematical model using Theorem’s RISC-V instruction and Linux process semantics. This means these proofs currently assume that the program runs as a single-threaded static binary with a fixed memory budget on a RISC-V CPU using Linux OS. Expanding the scope of these proofs is well within reach, as it would involve standardizing semantics for more assembly architectures and other operating system processes. These proofs operate on the compiled RISC-V instructions (i.e., executable binaries), and they comprise about 180 million lines of Rocq, with a typical proof running to about 600,000 lines to provide security guarantees on binaries with a median length of 18,000 RISC-V instructions. These proofs are built by translating the RISC-V assembly code to a mathematical model using Theorem’s RISC-V instruction and Linux process semantics. This means these proofs currently assume that the program runs as a single-threaded static binary with a fixed memory budget on a RISC-V CPU using Linux OS. Expanding the scope of these proofs is well within reach, as it would involve standardizing semantics for more assembly architectures and other operating system processes. See
an expert’s take
on the proofs Claude wrote.

blocks.text: Many of the bugs we found are ones that a fuzzer would be unlikely to ever find. Fuzzers mutate small inputs, typically capped at 1 MB, and typically rely on code coverage to guide them toward bugs. While proving an entry point in one library, Claude found a counter underflow in its copy of a decompressor that led to an out-of-bounds write, but only on inputs of around 20 MB that had one rare, specific layout. Other bugs include an out-of-bounds read in an image decoder that needed a 64 MB input and over 2 GB of memory, an out-of-bounds read in another library that needed a particular sequence of calls across two handles to the same file, and a rediscovery of CVE-2026-56132 in libexpat, which needed deeply nested input. Claude also found logic bugs that never crash at all. While proving that one library was memory-safe, for example, it noticed that a feature for restricting which files an application can load isn’t always enforced.

blocks.text: Proving more than memory safety

inlines.text: Proving more than memory safety

blocks.text: Proving that a fuzz test has no more crashes to find is more significant than it sounds. It’s common for fuzz tests in real-world code to test for violations of meaningful high-level properties, such as encode-decode roundtripping, idempotence, algebraic laws, differential testing, self-consistency, or equivalence to reference implementations. For example, a fuzz test for the LZO compression algorithm asserts that if you compress an input, then decompress it, the result is the same as the original. If the property does not hold, the program crashes—so proving the test never crashes is equivalent to proving the property itself.

For example, in order for Claude to complete its OSS-Fuzz proof for cpp-httplib, it was necessary to rule out the possibility of a stack overflow due to too much recursion in the std::set destructor. This recursion depth is bounded by the maximum depth of a tree, so Claude had to prove (on machine code!) that libc++’s red-black tree rebalancing algorithm is correctly optimized to keep the tree’s depth logarithmically bounded.

blocks.text: Other formal verification case studies

inlines.text: Other formal verification case studies

blocks.text: Formal verification is an expansive domain. The fuzz-test-to-proof example above is one instance of LLMs making formal verification more widely usable by directly applying proofs to machine code.

blocks.text: We’ve also seen success using LLMs with formal verification in other ways. For example, we asked Claude to write a formal spec of RFC 1950, the technical document that defines the zlib compression file format. Then, we had Claude prove that the zlib implementation in the Linux kernel correctly implements that spec. As with the examples above, Claude proved this property at the binary level, except instead of RISC-V, Claude directly proved the x86-compiled binary using Claude-generated (and heavily tested) formal semantics of the x86 ISA.7 We then repeated this process for half a dozen other widely used libraries. Along the way, we found some minor (unexploitable) bugs in corner cases, which are in the process of being filed upstream. We draw two conclusions from this exercise: (1) these extremely well-tested codebases are already almost fully correct, and (2) it is possible to prove end-to-end correctness properties about real existing codebases.

blocks.text: Proofs can be reused

inlines.text: Proofs can be reused

blocks.text: When agents work separately, they often end up duplicating a lot of effort. Proofs, like software, are recursively built from smaller proofs—and the smaller the proofs are, the more reusable they tend to be. To measure the impact of this, we let agents copy each other’s proofs as they worked on proving their own targets. When given access to this shared workspace, agents needed 17% fewer tokens than when they worked alone, and some agents even succeeded after previously failing in a solo attempt.

blocks.text: Limitations

inlines.text: Limitations

blocks.text: In practice, formal verification can sometimes prove less about the security of the code than we would like.

inlines.text: In practice, formal verification can sometimes prove less about the security of the code than we would like.

blocks.text: “Formally verified” does not mean “bug-free.” Claude can write a proof showing that a compiled program’s behavior satisfies the requirements of a formal spec (which is verified by an external proof checker). However, a proof checker can’t tell you whether your spec matches reality. To match reality, the spec must correctly encompass and model everything about the real-world machine that the verified program runs on, including the CPU and operating system. When bugs show up in verified code, it’s because the spec, or the assumed semantics of the machine, differs from reality. Fortunately, this also means we know where to look for remaining bugs, and how to design a system where those still-possibly-buggy gaps are minimized. Below are the ways this applies to our proofs, and ideas for future work that would close those gaps.

blocks.text: The claim may not cover everything we care about. We proved that a crash never triggers for any input under 64 MB on many fuzzing entry points in Google OSS-Fuzz, including ASan crashes. However, ASan doesn’t detect all memory safety bugs, and we didn’t verify all the entry points for each library. Even if we had, the whole library wouldn’t be covered by verifying all entry points (especially if there is dead code). Additionally, real programs might misuse the library, leading to memory corruption in the caller. To close that gap, we’d need to specify what callers must do for each public function, and callers would have to strictly adhere to it.

blocks.text: Conclusion

inlines.text: Conclusion

blocks.text: The trajectory is clear: formal verification, which was historically practical only for bespoke expert-crafted guarantees in the most safety-critical code, will soon be as practical as fuzzing is today for almost all production software. Just like static types, testing frameworks, and other correctness tooling, verification will mature from “bolted-on” to “built-in,” driven not only by LLMs but also by innovations in language design and development workflows.

blocks.text: In today’s world—where LLMs automatically scan for and find increasingly more code vulnerabilities—we must use processes that can guarantee code security properties. LLM-scaled formal verification is a promising approach toward securing these guarantees at a scope and scale that were previously unattainable. We encourage others to experiment so we can collectively build a world in which robust software has proliferated very widely and software bugs are a well-understood and quickly addressable rarity.
